questions.title: Solar power and grid access in India
questions.stem:
Text A — Buying capacity or buying power. India's solar auctions and investment in transmission illustrate a problem of coordination. In the practice state, generators compete for long contracts. Once connected, solar generation can displace fossil power during daylight. Several substations cannot carry all midday generation. Output the network cannot take is curtailed, and evening demand still relies partly on other sources.

Text B — Two proposals. A production subsidy would pay for each megawatt-hour delivered to the grid. Alternatively, public investment would upgrade a congested substation and storage connection. Independent producers can enter the auction, but small firms report expensive credit. Network users include households receiving a subsidised retail tariff and industrial users facing more frequent interruptions.

Text C — A planning exercise. The proposed grid upgrade costs 600 million rupees. The exercise holds gross generation fixed, excludes operating costs and assumes each extra MWh delivered displaces generation worth 1,500 rupees. Forecasts are annual steady-state values, not official Indian statistics. No environmental benefit has been included in that saving.

| Indicator | Existing grid | After upgrade |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross solar generation (MWh) | 500000 | 500000 |
| Electricity curtailed (MWh) | 100000 | 30000 |
| Employment in installation during construction | 0 | 450 |

Background reading: IEA, India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026. All district or scenario data and policy proposals are constructed for this paper.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Define a subsidy in the context of the production proposal.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Define investment as a component of aggregate demand.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate electricity delivered before and after the grid upgrade, and the percentage increase relative to initial delivery.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the annual value of generation displaced by the additional delivery under Text C's assumptions.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using a market diagram, explain how the production subsidy should affect the quantity of solar power delivered where the grid has spare capacity.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why a subsidy for additional installed capacity could yield smaller environmental benefits than anticipated in Text A.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using an AD–AS diagram, explain a possible long-run effect of more reliable grid infrastructure on industrial output.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why 450 construction jobs cannot by themselves establish an increase of 450 in total employment.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the texts, data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether the state should prioritise grid investment over a production subsidy.

steps.text: Financial support from government to a producer (1) that reduces its effective cost or increases the return per unit supplied (1). A transfer to the grid operator for a different purpose is not the per-unit payment described.
Spending on capital goods (1) that add to or replace productive capacity (1). Buying existing shares does not directly create this investment.
70,000 MWh × 1,500 rupees/MWh (1) = 105 million rupees per year (1). Credit a consistent own figure from the previous part.

On delivered solar price and quantity axes shift supply down/right by the subsidy. Mark original and new quantities and the gap between the price paid and price received (up to 2). A higher return per unit encourages production; with a responsive buyer and spare grid capacity equilibrium delivery rises (up to 2).

Installed capacity is potential generation. Midday curtailment prevents part of it from replacing fossil generation. Some accepted generation might displace another clean source. Environmental gain depends on actual marginal generation displaced; evening demand persists. Reward linked analysis grounded in the constraint.

Label price level and real GDP and shift the long-run supply curve right, or extend the full-employment part of a Keynesian curve (up to 2). Fewer outages reduce idle machine time and production losses, so firms can sustain higher output with existing inputs. A temporary construction job is not the long-run mechanism (up to 2).

Gross jobs count workers hired for the project. Some are already employed elsewhere; competing projects can lose workers or funding. A net increase depends on unemployment and spare skills. Construction posts also expire, so a one-off count does not measure permanent employment.

The grid upgrade adds 70,000 MWh of delivered power at unchanged gross generation. The assumed saving is 105 million rupees a year. Dividing the 600 million cost by that saving gives a simple payback of about 5.71 years before discounting, maintenance or environmental gains. More reliable service can also support industrial users.

A delivered-power subsidy can reward actual delivery and attract investment at less congested sites. It is weaker at a binding bottleneck where more panels cannot reach buyers. A uniform payment may favour firms with cheap credit. A single public upgrade faces construction delays and may serve few consumers if the forecast is wrong.

Prioritise the upgrade if curtailment persists, the asset lasts sufficiently long and displaced generation is genuinely costly. Target any production incentive at times or places of grid value. Evidence about evening storage, maintenance, alternative network routes and who pays could reverse the investment ranking.

The illustrative curtailment rates are 5% in the morning, 32% around midday and 8% later in the day. These percentages have different generation denominators: an unweighted mean is not the annual system rate.

Best fit, 0–15. 0: no relevant economics. 1–3: assertions or isolated concepts. 4–6: some relevant explanation, limited application. 7–9: coherent analysis with some application and consideration of consequences. 10–12: developed, applied analysis weighing competing considerations with a supported view. 13–15: precise theory and relevant diagrams where useful, evidence integrated throughout, and a balanced judgement that explains conditions or relative importance. Other defensible conclusions can receive full credit.

questions.title: Tourism receipts and inclusion in Jamaica
questions.stem:
Text A — Visitors and livelihoods. Jamaica's experience of a pandemic-related tourism interruption illustrates the risks of dependence on international travel. In the practice coastal district, reopened hotels generate foreign receipts. Some hotel groups import food under long contracts. Small local farms could supply more, but they lack cold storage and consistent certification. Hotel wages and job security differ across permanent and seasonal posts.

Text B — A development choice. The district could market additional visitor packages or co-finance cold storage and help farms meet buyers' standards. Marketing is quick to launch. More visitors could add pressure to a beach used by fishers and residents, while improved storage would also serve domestic markets. Land title requirements could exclude some small growers from the grant.

Text C — Interpreting receipts. The practice accounts cover only visitors' spending and imported inputs used directly to deliver tourist services. They exclude profit repatriation, subsequent rounds of spending and other industries. These are constructed district data, not national accounts.

| District indicator | Year 1 | Year 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visitor arrivals (thousands) | 400 | 480 |
| Spending per visitor (US dollars) | 900 | 850 |
| Imported inputs for visitor services (US dollar million) | 108 | 144 |
| Permanent local hotel jobs | 7200 | 7350 |

Background reading: IMF, Jamaica Article IV consultation (2025). All district or scenario data and policy proposals are constructed for this paper.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Define a leakage from the circular flow of income and give one example from Text A.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate gross visitor receipts in each year and their percentage growth.

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in visitor receipts after subtracting the imported inputs in the table.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using a foreign exchange diagram, explain the likely effect of additional foreign visitor spending on the Jamaican dollar in a floating exchange market, other things equal.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain why increased demand for hotel meals might lead to only a small increase in local farm incomes in the short run.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Using a negative externality diagram, explain why the unregulated number of beach visits may exceed the socially efficient number.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain why the change in permanent hotel employment is insufficient evidence of a comparable improvement in household welfare.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Using the texts, data and your knowledge of economics, evaluate whether co-financing local food supply chains would support more inclusive development than additional tourism marketing.

steps.text: A sustained improvement in people's living standards or well-being (1), involving qualitative dimensions such as health, education, opportunity or distribution (1). An increase in GDP alone is insufficient.
Income withdrawn from the domestic expenditure stream (1). Spending on imported food is one example (1); accept a valid explanation of imports from the extract.
Year 1: 360 − 108 = US$252 million; Year 2: 408 − 144 = US$264 million (1 for consistent working). Increase = US$12 million (1). This is not GDP or the complete current-account balance.

Quote foreign currency per Jamaican dollar and use quantity of Jamaican dollars on the horizontal axis. Shift demand for Jamaican dollars right; show appreciation (up to 2). Visitors or their payment intermediaries exchange foreign currency for local goods and services. An equivalent correctly inverted quotation earns credit (up to 2).

Long-term import contracts limit short-run substitution. Cold storage and certification constrain local supply even when hotels want fresh produce. Revenue can initially flow to overseas suppliers rather than local farms. Credit linked reasoning about timing and the conditions for a later local gain.

Define a visit as the unit. Draw demand and private marginal cost and put marginal social cost above private cost for crowding or damage imposed on others. Mark Qsocial below Qmarket (up to 2). The private decision leaves out costs to fishers or residents; extra visits between these quantities cost society more than they benefit users (up to 2). Accept a consistent external cost of consumption diagram.

Permanent jobs rose by 150, much less proportionately than arrivals. Job count omits real pay, distribution, insecure seasonal work and environmental costs. More jobs can raise welfare, but household income and access to shared resources matter too. Credit a linked comparison using the context.

Arrivals rose by 20%, but lower spending per visitor restricted receipts growth to 13.33%. After imported inputs the increase was only US$12 million. Local cold storage can reduce waste and allow farms to compete for hotel contracts, spreading income to rural workers. It can serve residents even when visitor demand falls.

Infrastructure may be underused unless quality, delivery schedules and contract terms suit hotels. Title requirements could concentrate gains among established owners. Marketing can quickly support employment when there is slack, but an extra visitor can increase imported input demand and pressure a crowded beach. The partial accounts cannot establish total local value added.

Where arrivals have recovered and procurement is the bottleneck, favour shared storage with access for small or tenant growers and measurable procurement targets. Where rooms are empty through weak demand, limited marketing may yield quicker gains. Test progress using farm incomes, local purchases, wages and environmental costs, not arrivals alone.

Illustrative local procurement shares are 66% for small hotels, 46% for medium hotels and 27% for large hotels. The gap identifies a possible market for farms; neither causation nor the volume of possible new orders follows from these shares alone.

Best fit, 0–15. 0: no relevant economics. 1–3: assertions or isolated concepts. 4–6: some relevant explanation, limited application. 7–9: coherent analysis with some application and consideration of consequences. 10–12: developed, applied analysis weighing competing considerations with a supported view. 13–15: precise theory and relevant diagrams where useful, evidence integrated throughout, and a balanced judgement that explains conditions or relative importance. Other defensible conclusions can receive full credit.
